newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Barings gives ING a world profile.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Barings gives ING a world profile.

text.p: If ING Groep chairman Aad Jacobs needed any indication of how the Dutch financial services giant is perceived around the world, it came in a recent meeting with a Chinese politican.
Jacobs was eager to raise the issue of ING's long-standing application for an insurance licence in China, a move which would open up a market of 1.2 billion people.
"But he was only interested in one thing...Barings," Jacobs recalled in an interview before jetting off to another far-flung corner of ING's global empire.
Jacobs, a 60-year-old former investment analyst, mentions Barings with apparently mixed feelings.
ING bought the venerable British merchant bank for 1.7 billion guilders ($899.7 million) in March 1995, swooping after it collapsed from rogue trader Nick Leeson's derivatives trading losses.
But analysts say Barings attracts an inordinately large amount of attention in relation to its size within ING, which had total assets of 465 billion guilders at end-September.
Instead they laud Jacobs for his success in continuing the integration of the insurance and banking businesses which merged to form ING in 1991 and for focusing on profitability.

Jacobs, who hails from the Nationale Nederlanden insurance operations which combined with those of NMB Postbank, took up his current position in September 1992 after his predecesser resigned amid a share deal controversy.
Surprised at his own appointment, others saw him as a logical replacement because he was untainted by the scandal.
He retires in less than two years.

"He may well be remembered for Barings," says Andrew Goodwin, analyst at UBS in London. "But, in terms of his overall achievements, it's more significant in terms of the improvement in underlying profitability."
ACHIEVEMENTS SINCE 1991
Looking back on ING's achievements since 1991, Jacobs proudly lists the fourfold increase in market capitalisation and annual earnings growth in excess of his 10 percent target.
Net profit in the first nine months of 1996 was 2.34 billion guilders, 25 percent above the same year-earlier period.
Valued at $24.2 billion, ING is the third largest Dutch-listed company behind Royal Dutch Petroleum, part of Royal Dutch/Shell, and Unilever.
It ranks ahead of brewer Heineken and Philips Electronics, although their brands are much better known around the world.

When the merger was announced, critics claimed that combining the conservative world of insurance with the more entrepreneurial world of banking would produce a clash of cultures and bring little reward to shareholders.
Since then there have been few other successful bank/insurance mergers, with the exception of Dutch-Belgian group Fortis.
"A lot of people were sceptical five years ago. Now we hardly hear any complaints," Jacobs says.
JACOBS SATISFIED WITH PERFORMANCE
Although Barings' returns have fallen short of targets so far, Jacobs remains satisfied with its performance.
He acknowledges that the Chinese official's awareness of ING as the owner of Barings is part of a worldwide phenomenon.

"Commercially, it did much better than we ever expected. It gave us worldwide recognition. We are invited on the banking side for deals we could never have dreamed of two or three years ago. They have excellent people," he said.
Now ING is often invited into banking syndicates for large infrastructure projects and private loans.
Analysts agree, saying the deal brought ING publicity which raised its global profile.
"The price was a little too high," says IRIS analyst Bart ven der Feen, adding however that the timing was right.
He says Barings offers ING exposure to high-growth emerging markets, where the British bank has a particular strength.
Harry Luchtenveld of Generale Bank said ING subsidiaries around the world preferred to operate under their own name at the time of the merger rather than the little known ING name.
"Now every subsidiary is proud to include ING and its lion emblem in their own names," he said. ($ = 1.889 Dutch Guilders)
